## The Push You Can Feel Through Nothing

Push two magnets together the wrong way and something invisible pushes back. Your hand feels it. Nothing is touching. This bothered scientists for centuries, and honestly it should bother you a little too.

Every magnet has two ends called **poles**: north and south. The rule is short and absolute — **opposite poles attract, like poles repel**. Bring two north poles together and they shove apart no matter how hard you press.

Here is a fact that surprises almost everyone: **you cannot make a magnet with only one pole.** Cut a bar magnet exactly in half hoping to separate north from south, and you do not get two halves. You get two complete smaller magnets, each with its own north and south. Cut those in half and it happens again. Physicists have searched hard for a single isolated pole — a magnetic monopole — and have never confirmed one.

The invisible push is described as a **magnetic field**: a region around the magnet where magnetic force acts. Sprinkle iron filings on paper over a magnet and they arrange into curved lines running pole to pole. You are not seeing the field itself — fields are not made of stuff — but you are seeing its shape.

Only a few materials are strongly magnetic. Iron, nickel, and cobalt are the common ones, which is why a refrigerator magnet grabs a steel door (steel is mostly iron) but slides right off an aluminum can, a copper pipe, or a gold ring. If a magnet does not stick to something metal, that is real information about which metal it is.

Now the connection that runs the modern world. In 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted noticed a compass needle twitch whenever he switched on a nearby electric current. Electricity and magnetism are not two separate phenomena — they are two faces of one thing. Coil a wire around an iron nail and run current through it and you have built an **electromagnet**, whose enormous advantage is that it can be switched OFF. That single property runs junkyard cranes, doorbells, speakers, hard drives, and every electric motor you have ever used.

And Earth itself is a giant magnet, generated by molten iron churning in its core. That is why a compass works. One last strange detail: the thing your compass calls "north" is physically a magnetic *south* pole — because opposite poles attract, and the needle's north end is being pulled toward it. Scientists have known about this naming joke for centuries and simply kept it.

## The Push You Can Feel Through Nothing

Hold two bar magnets near one another. You can feel a push or pull before they touch. That is a force acting across a gap.

A simple bar magnet has north and south **poles**. With the magnets held aligned, opposite facing poles **attract** and like facing poles **repel**. A freely turning magnet can rotate, changing which poles face each other.

Imagine dividing a bar magnet across its middle. Each piece becomes a smaller magnet with both poles; this does not isolate a north-only or south-only magnet. Treat this as a thought experiment, not a cutting activity.

A **magnetic field** describes magnetic influence at each location. Field lines are a model of direction and relative strength, not physical threads. Iron filings can reveal a pattern because they become magnetized and align with the local field. Use a sealed field viewer for a classroom observation. Outside a bar magnet, field direction runs from north to south; inside it returns from south to north.

Iron, nickel and cobalt are familiar strongly magnetic materials at ordinary temperatures. Many steels are strongly attracted, but some stainless steels are not. Aluminum, copper, pure gold and ordinary plastic do not stick to a stationary classroom magnet. Their weak magnetic responses are different from the strong attraction in this test. Alloys matter: a U.S. copper-nickel five-cent coin does not behave like pure nickel. A sticking test gives evidence about a material, but cannot identify its composition by itself.

Electric **current** produces a magnetic field. A current-carrying coil forms an **electromagnet**, often strengthened by a soft iron core. Changing the current changes the field. Opening the circuit stops the coil current, although the core may keep some magnetism. More turns can strengthen a coil when current and geometry are comparable; adding wire also changes resistance. Use only the teacher-approved current-limited kit described in the activity.

Electromagnets help cranes lift and release steel. Release must still be tested: residual magnetism or tangled objects can keep a load attached. Permanent magnets can also be used in devices with mechanical release mechanisms. Speakers use a changing coil current interacting with a magnetic field to move a cone.

Earth’s main field is sustained by motion of electrically conducting fluid in its liquid outer **core**. The inner core is solid. A **compass** aligns with the horizontal component of the local magnetic field, which usually differs from true geographic north. Near the northern magnetic region, the field enters Earth, so that region behaves like a bar magnet’s south pole. Magnetic and geographic poles are not the same locations.

from: A junkyard crane picks up a car, moves it, then drops it. Explain why an electromagnet is required for this job and a permanent magnet would not work.
to: Explain why a controllable electromagnet is useful for lifting and releasing steel. Could a permanent-magnet design also release a load?

from: The crane has to RELEASE the car. An electromagnet is only magnetic while current flows, so cutting the current drops the load. A permanent magnet would hold the car and could not let go on command.
to: Switching off coil current reduces the electromagnet’s field, helping release steel. Residual magnetism and tangled objects can affect release, so it must be tested. A permanent magnet can also release a load with a mechanical stripper or other release mechanism.

from: Place a paperclip on a table and slowly bring a magnet near without touching it — the clip jumps. Or hold a magnet under a sheet of paper or a table and move a clip on top. The magnet moves the clip across a gap, so the force crosses empty space.
to: Bring a classroom magnet toward a steel paperclip while keeping a visible air gap. The clip can move before contact. This demonstrates magnetic force at a distance through air; it does not by itself test a vacuum.

from: Is there such a thing as a one-pole magnet?
to: Does dividing a bar magnet separate its north and south poles?

from: None has ever been confirmed. Some theories predict magnetic monopoles should exist, and physicists have run serious searches for them, but so far every magnet ever cut has produced two poles.
to: No. In this thought experiment, each piece is a smaller magnet with north and south poles. This result does not require physically cutting a magnet.

from: Barely — living tissue is very weakly repelled by strong fields. Scientists have levitated a live frog in an extremely powerful magnet, which is real and as strange as it sounds. The frog was unharmed.
to: Most body tissue has a very weak diamagnetic response: it is weakly repelled by a strong, nonuniform magnetic field. That is very different from iron sticking strongly to a classroom magnet.

from: Design a device that pulls steel items out of a mixed recycling bin and then releases them into a separate container. Use the lesson's rules about materials, fields, and electromagnets, and test your design against a mixed pile.
to: Design a small tabletop sorter that picks steel paperclips from a clean mixed sample and releases them into a tray. Use a teacher-approved classroom electromagnet kit or demonstrate a permanent magnet with a mechanical release. Test pickup and release separately.

from: Your school's recycling bins mix steel cans, aluminum cans, plastic bottles, and paper. The custodian sorts them by hand, which takes an hour a day. You have magnets, insulated wire, batteries, iron nails, cardboard, string, and tape.
to: Model recycling with five carbon-steel paperclips, clean aluminum-foil pieces, plastic counters and paper pieces on a tray. Available materials are a teacher-approved current-limited low-voltage electromagnet kit, a classroom magnet, cardboard, string and tape. Use the kit’s supplied switch and instructions; do not connect loose wire directly across a battery.

from: How can we build a device that lifts only the steel out of a mixed bin and then drops it exactly where we want it, using what we know about magnetic materials and fields?
to: How can a tabletop device pick out the steel paperclips and then release them into a separate tray?

**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Hold two magnets close and you can feel something pushing back through empty air. Nothing is touching. That push is a **field**, and fields are one of the strangest true things in physics.

1. Read **The Push You Can Feel Through Nothing**.
2. Learn the terms in the **Glossary**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Word Scramble**.
3. Keep the **Magnet Rules** chart open while you experiment.
4. Sort the materials in **Will It Stick?** — three of these surprise people.
5. Practise explaining with **Magnet Frames**, then check yourself against the rubric.
6. Take the quiz. Question 4 is the one almost everyone gets wrong.
7. If your class has the **Magnetism Lab** in the STEM Lab, run the Field Walk challenge and find the hidden magnet.
8. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Rules of the Invisible** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
9. Finish with **Design Challenge: A Sorter That Lets Go** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.

One rule for this lesson: every time you predict, say it OUT LOUD before you test. Being wrong out loud is how physics gets learned. 🧲

Picture panels: Facing poles and forces; Two poles and a field; A controlled coil; A compass and Earth’s core. All artwork is text-free. Native captions define the model: coral denotes north, teal denotes south in magnet and compass diagrams. Colors do not identify real materials or polarity. Object identity and alloy are supplied by the card text, not established by appearance. The coin is a deliberately plain silhouette, not a reproduction of a minted design. Sorting predicts sticking to an ordinary stationary classroom magnet; weak magnetic responses and moving-field effects are outside that activity. Force arrows differ from field-direction arrows as each caption explains. Core rings and field curves are schematic. The split-magnet image is a thought experiment, not an instruction to break magnets. Circuit pictures explain switching and are not build plans; use only the teacher-approved current-limited classroom kit or a non-electrical model. A core can retain magnetism after current stops. Educator review is pending.
